<reason>A tight, high-quality clash that narrowed to one question: in the gap where a judge finds credible evidence of imminent gun risk but no arrest, hold, or protective order is available, should the guns stay? CON built a genuinely sharp case (the leftover-risk dilemma, the notice/triggering contradiction, the "implies, not requires" safeguard attack, the Maryland doorway death as an irreversible error), and PRO conceded real ground on statutory design. But when PRO's pressure question forced the issue, CON answered "Yes—he keeps the guns," and its "Neither" to Q2 collapsed into the same answer. Since the motion itself stipulates credible evidence of imminent risk, CON's reply that such evidence "is not evidence of imminence" if it fails other thresholds reads as redefining the motion's premise rather than answering it, and its claim that existing tools already cover every real case is asserted more than shown. PRO answered the triggering contradiction adequately (timing: dangerous while guns in reach, less lethal after) and kept the guns-are-the-distinctive-lethal-channel point live against the borrowed-gun/truck reply. PRO's closing crystallized the choice ("a veto that the victim must bleed before a judge may act") more decisively than CON's "lowering the floor" reframe. CON's clipped final rebuttal is a minor execution cost. Clear but competitive PRO win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Pressure Q1 and follow-through: asking whether the court must leave the guns in the house when evidence is insufficient for arrest or a hold, extracting CON's "Yes—he keeps the guns" in B4.1, then converting that into the closing's decisive frame that CON's rule is "possession until the first attempt." CON's contradiction attack (B2.1/B3.1) was the strongest counter-pressure, but PRO's timing answer in A4.1 defused it enough to keep its route alive.</best_rebuttal>
